transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Um... well, what brings me in is that I've been waking up with this heavy, hollow sadness. It's like... like the studio lights are on but there's no music in me anymore. I actually just got new lights installed in the studio last month. They're these LED ones that are supposed to mimic natural daylight, you know? Because the old fluorescents were giving me terrible migraines, especially during the winter showcase rehearsals. We were doing this piece inspired by Swan Lake, but with a modern twist, and the costumes were this gorgeous deep teal... but anyway, yeah, I just feel really empty inside right now.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let's see... I guess the depressed part has been going on for about nine months now. I remember because it started right around the time I was choreographing a new contemporary piece for the summer festival. We were using this really beautiful instrumental track with heavy cello. 

I actually started taking cello lessons myself a few years ago because I wanted to understand the musical phrasing better for my choreography. My instructor, David, told me I had a good ear but terrible posture for it, which is hilarious because I'm a dancer, right? You'd think my posture would be flawless. But sitting with a cello is just completely different than holding your core at the barre, it really strains your left shoulder... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, the sadness. It's been about nine months of feeling this way.
Have you ever experienced periods where your mood was unusually elevated, you had more energy than usual, or you felt like you didn’t need much sleep?

Yeah, um... elevated? I guess so. There were stretches before this where I just felt dazzlingly alive, you know? Like I could choreograph an entire ballet in a weekend. I actually did try that once, back when I was working with this incredible contemporary company in Seattle. It rains so much there, which you'd think would be depressing, but I loved it. I bought this bright yellow raincoat, like the classic fisherman style, and I'd walk to the studio just listening to the rain hit the hood. It sounded like tap dancing. I used to tap when I was a kid. My mom made me take tap and ballet, but I always hated the tap shoes because the metal taps would get scuffed and she'd make me polish them... 

But anyway, yeah, I'd have these periods where I was just buzzing with energy. And then, out of nowhere, I'd get so furious. Like, if anyone even questioned my vision for a piece, or if they reminded me that I was supposed to be resting my ankle—because I had this minor sprain from landing a grand jeté weirdly on a slippery floor—I would just snap. It was like going from fireworks to a thunderstorm in two seconds.
How long did those periods of elevated mood and increased energy typically last?

Well, the elevated part... that whole pattern really started right after that ankle injury I mentioned, and it's been going on for about two months now. Which is actually kind of a relief, because for a while I was terrified I'd never dance again. You know how it is with injuries, they just mess with your head so much. I had to go to physical therapy twice a week, and my therapist, Sarah, she was amazing. She had this golden retriever named Barnaby who would sit in the clinic and just watch everyone do their exercises. He was the sweetest dog, he had this one floppy ear that never stood up right. I actually thought about getting a dog myself because I live alone now, and the apartment gets so quiet... but then I realized I travel too much for choreography gigs, and it wouldn't be fair to a pet. I did buy some succulents, though. They're supposed to be impossible to kill, but I somehow managed to drown the aloe vera plant... 

But yeah, so it's been about two months since all that energy and the snapping at people started.
When you had those periods of elevated mood and increased energy, did they last for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least four days in a row?

Yeah, I mean... it definitely felt like it was all day, every day. Like I was just plugged into a socket and couldn't unplug. I remember waking up at, like, 3 AM and just starting to sketch out lighting designs for this piece I was working on. I actually got really into lighting design for a minute there. I bought all these gels—you know, the colored films they put over stage lights? I had them taped all over my apartment windows to see how the natural light would filter through them at different times of day. It made the living room look like a stained glass window, which was gorgeous, but my landlord was furious because the tape left this sticky residue on the glass. I tried using rubbing alcohol to get it off, but the smell was so overpowering I had to open all the windows, and then a bird flew in! A literal pigeon just swooped right into my kitchen. I spent two hours trying to coax it back out with some stale bread I had meant to throw away... 

But, um... wait, what did you ask? Oh, right, four days. Yeah, it was definitely longer than four days. It felt like weeks of just... non-stop going.
During those periods of elevated mood and high energy, did it ever cause problems in your work, relationships, or daily life?

Problems? Well, yeah, I guess so. I fell way behind on my teaching prep, which is so unlike me because I'm usually meticulous about my syllabi. But I just couldn't focus on it, and then I completely missed this huge grant deadline. It was the National Endowment for the Arts grant, which is incredibly competitive, and I had all these grand ideas for a site-specific piece in an abandoned warehouse. I actually went to scout this one warehouse down by the waterfront, and it was perfect—exposed brick, these massive industrial windows, and the acoustics were incredible. I brought a portable speaker and just played this haunting cello piece to hear how it echoed. But the place was freezing. I had to wear my puffy coat the whole time, and I ended up getting a terrible cold afterward. I drank so much tea with honey, but it turned out the honey I bought was this weird infused kind with lavender, which sounded nice but tasted like soap... 

But anyway, yeah, work got really chaotic. My studio was just a disaster zone of sketches and costume fabrics, and eventually, my collaborators just stepped in and started handling all the basic scheduling for me because I couldn't keep track of anything. I mean, I'm still showing up for the essential stuff, the actual rehearsals, but I'm definitely not functioning like I normally do as a choreographer or a teacher right now.
Can you recall if any of those elevated mood periods lasted for at least a full week without stopping?

Well, yeah, like I was saying earlier, this whole pattern really started right after that ankle injury, and it's just been going on for about two months now. It hasn't really stopped. Which is funny, because before the injury, I was actually planning this trip to Japan to study Butoh dancing. Have you ever seen Butoh? It's this incredible, avant-garde Japanese dance form, very slow and controlled, usually performed with white body makeup. I was so fascinated by the control it requires, which is ironic because I feel like I have zero control right now. I even bought this special white powder makeup online to practice, but it got everywhere. My bathroom looked like a powdered sugar explosion, and the worst part was it somehow got into the grout of the tiles. I spent hours scrubbing it with an old toothbrush. I had to buy a new toothbrush, obviously, and I ended up getting one of those electric ones that buzzes every thirty seconds to tell you to switch quadrants. It's actually really helpful, but the buzzing sound is so loud it scares my downstairs neighbor's cat... 

But yeah, two months. It's definitely been going on for two months straight.

During that time when you felt so energized and couldn’t sleep, did things ever get so out of control that you had to be hospitalized, or was there a time when people around you were seriously concerned about your behavior to the point where you couldn’t function normally in your daily life?

Hospitalized? No, no, I've never been hospitalized for this. I mean, my collaborators were definitely concerned, like I said, they had to take over my scheduling because I was just all over the place. But I wasn't, like, completely unable to function. I was still going to rehearsals. I just couldn't sit still long enough to do the paperwork. Paperwork is honestly the worst part of being a choreographer anyway. You spend all this time trying to secure funding and write these artist statements that sound so pretentious. I had to write one last year that asked how my work "interrogates the liminal space of the human condition." Like, what does that even mean? I ended up using this online thesaurus just to find bigger words, and I think I used the word "juxtaposition" about twelve times. I actually love looking up words, though. Did you know the word "choreography" comes from the Greek words for "dance" and "writing"? It's literally dance-writing. Which makes sense, because sometimes I feel like I'm writing a novel with my body, you know? Except right now, it's more like a really chaotic comic book. 

But no, to answer your question, I didn't have to go to a hospital or anything. People were worried, sure, but I was still doing my art.
